Andariel, a couple of things: First, the motto of the Foundation is "Secure, Contain, Protect", not "Destroy, Destroy, Destroy". Second, as Voct said, there's an unknown force actingg on this thing animating it in a clearly anomalous manner that the Foundation can't explain. Although you're certainly free to feel that it can/should be neutralized, realize that the Foundation tends to be paranoid and generally unwilling to upset the status quo if they've got something successfully contained. Especially with something that acts alive, they could provoke it into doing something new and unexpected.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The skeletal mount used as an illustration for this SCP is that of Monolophosaurus jiangi and a fiberglass one at that (Allosaurus for comparison). A rule of thumb for determining if a mount has fossil bone or at least plaster casts of them is to look for the metallic armature holding the bones/replicas as is the case with the Tyrannosaurus specimen "Sue". With fiberglass replicas, people figured out they could thread the supporting structure through the "bones".

This leaves this SCP in a bit of a pickle. I'm not sure that most museum curators would condone partial destruction of their specimens to assemble a seamless mount. Probably the ruckus caused by someone getting sacked/killed for not complying with common practice would alert the Foundation.

@Deadlymoose: Linnaean ranks are a rather poor measure of diversity or morphological disparity. True, you do need to go past a lot of forks in the tree of life to get from A. to T. but there is a good deal of common morphological ground between the two or they wouldn't be both tetanurans.
Museums do use real fossil bone in their mounts, if it's been preserved adequately by applying synthetic resins.

item.title: Re: While I'm nitpicking
item.content:encoded:
What other museums do has nothing at all to do with the issue. Frankly, if one museum wants to violate generally accepted museum mores, it doesn't need anyone's permission. Foundation personnel would understand this, and while they might raise an eyebrow, unless they found a piece of paper in the museum where the skeleton was located directly stating "WE DID NOT USE REAL BONES FOR DISPLAY OH FUCK" they would not make any assumptions on that front, and it would not be mentioned in the article.

What the Foundation knows is that for some reason this display model skeleton seems to be 1) animate, and 2) made of real dinosaur bones. These are the facts that made it into the article. That is good and proper.

Any further information would be either magic knowledge the Foundation would not have access to, which would be poor form on voct's part OOC, or conjecture based on unrelated external factors (IE the policies of other museums unrelated to the SCP object or its effect), which has absolutely no place in the article IC.

Either way, to give a further explanation on that point would be detrimental to the presentation of the article, and furthermore from what I see the author doesn't want to and it's his article, damn.

which has been assessed by Foundation herpetologists as being well within theoretical norms for an allosaurus.

That would be pretty incompetent of the Foundation, considering dinosaurs had very little in common with modern-day reptiles and much more in common with modern-day birds (which are distantly related to Allosaurus, in fact) and mammals. Wouldn't that just be 'paleontologists'?

item.title: Re: While I'm nitpicking
item.content:encoded:
Putting things in an article that there's no way or reason for the narrator to know is bad writing, oh my children.

Except you'd think the Foundation might have a paleontologist or two on staff.

Or, you know, someone who knows anything about museums. Considering they did an investigation of the museum and all.

So no, adding some kind of reference to that would not be bad writing.

Again, obviously readers who don't know anything about this (paleontology/museums) aren't going to get how unlikely this is, and so it won't seem contrived to them. To me, personally, who cares about the subject far more than the average person, it seems contrived. It seems like it's there because the out-of-universe authors didn't know it, but in-universe the Foundation researchers ought to have twigged on to it at some point during their investigation because it is that unusual.

Hope that clarifies things. It isn't hurting the article for most people, so take it or leave it.

item.title: While I'm nitpicking
item.content:encoded: Museums don't usually put actual dinosaur bones on display. They put replicas up. The bones themselves are almost priceless and will decay on display and are usually pretty fragile and are heavy as fuck. Some smaller collections do put up a few of the actual bones themselves, but it's rare, and I'll bet you anything that a full mounted Allosaurus skeleton is going to be replica entirely.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
By the way, side note on this, because I'm a huge dinosaur nerd and thus this annoys the shit out me. :P

TL;DR WARNING

#1: Allosaurus is an entirely different genus from Tyrannosaurus, so that isn't a species variation. (Protip: Allosaurus fragilis is genus Allosaurus, species fragilis. Tyrannosaurus rex is genus Tyrannosaurus, species rex.)
#2: While both were apex predators, and theropods, the similarity ends there. Allosaurus was a carnosaur, while Tyrannosaurus was a coelurosaur (same as modern birds). They were separated in time by 80 million years. I know the skeletons look vaguely similar to the (massively :P) untrained eye, but that's like saying rhinoceros are basically the same as horses with a horn added. Or humans are basically the same as monkeys. Actually, no, scratch that, we're much closer related to monkeys than allosaurids were to tyrannosaurids. Maybe tarsiers (different infraorders, same suborders). But even then, we're alive at the same time as tarsiers as opposed to 80 million years later, so…
#3: The examples you linked from the article are more like not realizing lions and tigers were the same genus because they have a couple significantly different characteristics.

In summary, Allosaurus is a very big difference from Tyrannosaurus. This is srs bsns paleontology. Yo.
